newsitem.title: USA: Rebel leader's wife leaves compound in Texas siege.
newsitem.headline: Rebel leader's wife leaves compound in Texas siege.

text.p: The wife of Texas separatist leader Richard McLaren on Saturday left the mountain compound where her husband and a handful of his armed supporters were under siege from elite police units.

Evelyn McLaren walked out of the dilapidated compound at around 11 a.m. (1600 GMT) on the seventh day of a standoff between the self-styled Republic of Texas group and scores of police in the remote Davis Mountains of west Texas.
"She is out of the compound, she is safe and she's talking with her lawyer right now," her brother, J.C. Mason, told reporters. "She is in good hands."
Evelyn McLaren's two daughters, who had made an impassioned plea for her to get out of harm's way, joyously hugged each other at a roadblock about 10 miles (15 km) away.

On Friday they urged Richard McLaren -- who is their stepfather -- to surrender or, failing that, at least persuade Evelyn to leave. Their tearful pleas were broadcast on television and radio and police sent letters and photographs from the daughters into the compound.
Richard McLaren and five other Republic members remained inside on Saturday, surrounded by police units and refusing pleas to surrender.
Five of the six face state felony charges, and police Special Weapons and Tactics (SWAT) teams advanced to within 440 yards (metres) of the compound late on Friday.

The Republic of Texas, which formed in 1995 and has ties to militias, holds that the 1845 annexation of Texas by the United States was illegal. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after breaking away from Mexico in 1836 in a rebellion that McLaren likens to his own.
The deployment panicked the Republic members, who claim Texas is an independent nation and that they form its provisional government.

"Mayday, mayday, mayday, hostiles invading Republic of Texas embassy. We have hostiles in the woods. This is a mayday call to any nation of the world. We are being invaded," McLaren cried out over shortwave radio when the police moved in.

State officials said one rebel was heard over shortwave radio ordering others to open fire on the advancing units, but no shots were fired and, after a quiet night, police were encouraged by Evelyn McLaren's decision to leave the compound.

"Perhaps that will encourage others to do the same and we are certainly willing to wait to give them that chance," Laureen Chernow, spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Public Safety, told reporters.
"We are trying to give everyone the opportunity to think things over, come out and, if they are charged, to have their day in court," Chernow said.

But McLaren, a 43-year-old vintner from Missouri, has shown no sign of preparing to surrender and was in a defiant mood when police forces moved within striking distance of his "embassy" compound on Friday.
"We'll take a good hunk of you boys with us," he was heard shouting in the shortwave radio tape.

As many as 200 heavily armed police have surrounded the rebel base since the siege began on Sunday when the Republic group seized two hostages in retaliation for the arrest of its security chief, Robert Scheidt.
The hostages were later released in exchange for Scheidt, who on Friday became the first rebel to walk out of the ramshackle compound and surrender to police.
Scheidt and five of those still inside the compound face felony charges of engaging in criminal activities, and three of them are also charged with aggravated kidnapping.
Evelyn McLaren faces no criminal charges but Mason, her brother, said police planned to question her for up to 72 hours before releasing her.
